blocks.en: "...but as He who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, because it is written, 'Be holy, for I am holy.'" — 1 Peter 1:15-16 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...como aquel que os llamó es santo, sed también vosotros santos en toda vuestra manera de vivir; porque escrito está: Sed santos, porque yo soy santo." — 1 Pedro 1:15-16 (RVG)

blocks.en: Gird Up Your Mind, Set Your Hope
blocks.es_reference: Ceñid la Mente, Poned la Esperanza

blocks.en: "Therefore." With that one word Peter turns from what God has done to how the believer must now live. Because of the living hope, the inheritance, and the salvation he has just described, he says, "gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and rest your hope fully upon the grace that is to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 1:13). In Peter's day a man tucked up his long robe into his belt before he ran or worked, so that nothing would trip him. To "gird up the loins of your mind" is to pull in the loose, lazy thinking and make the mind ready for action. Be sober — clear-headed, not intoxicated by the world. And fix your hope, fully and finally, not on the comforts of this life but on the grace that is coming when Christ appears. The hope born in us at the new birth is meant to shape the way we think and live right now.
blocks.es_reference: "Por tanto." Con esa sola palabra Pedro pasa de lo que Dios ha hecho a cómo debe ahora vivir el creyente. A causa de la esperanza viva, la herencia, y la salvación que acaba de describir, dice: "ceñid los lomos de vuestro entendimiento, sed sobrios, y esperad por completo en la gracia que se os traerá cuando Jesucristo sea manifestado" (1 Pedro 1:13). En tiempos de Pedro un hombre recogía su larga túnica en el cinto antes de correr o trabajar, para que nada lo hiciera tropezar. "Ceñir los lomos del entendimiento" es recoger el pensamiento suelto y perezoso y disponer la mente para la acción. Sed sobrios — de mente clara, no embriagados por el mundo. Y fijad vuestra esperanza, plena y finalmente, no en las comodidades de esta vida sino en la gracia que viene cuando Cristo aparezca. La esperanza nacida en nosotros en el nuevo nacimiento ha de moldear nuestra manera de pensar y vivir ahora mismo.

blocks.en: Be Holy, for I Am Holy
blocks.es_reference: Sed Santos, porque Yo Soy Santo

blocks.en: From that settled hope Peter issues his great command. "As obedient children, not conforming yourselves to the former lusts, as in your ignorance; but as He who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct" (1 Peter 1:14-15). Once we lived in the desires of our ignorance; now, as obedient children, we are not to be poured back into that old mold. Instead we are to be holy — set apart, clean, like our Father — "because it is written, 'Be holy, for I am holy'" (Leviticus 11:44). The standard is nothing less than the character of God Himself.
blocks.es_reference: Desde esa esperanza firme Pedro lanza su gran mandamiento. "Como hijos obedientes, no os conforméis a los deseos que teníais antes en vuestra ignorancia; sino, como aquel que os llamó es santo, sed también vosotros santos en toda vuestra manera de vivir" (1 Pedro 1:14-15). Antes vivíamos en los deseos de nuestra ignorancia; ahora, como hijos obedientes, no hemos de ser vaciados de nuevo en aquel viejo molde. Más bien hemos de ser santos — apartados, limpios, como nuestro Padre — "porque escrito está: Sed santos, porque yo soy santo" (Levítico 11:44). La norma no es menos que el carácter de Dios mismo.

blocks.en: Here the lesson must speak plainly, for we have grown comfortable. As Christians we have too often made peace with "pretty good" instead of holiness. We can all quote, "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23) — but that verse describes the lost man's need, and we must not turn it into an excuse for the believer to settle into sin. We expect the world to compromise; the Christian does not have to. We will never be happy, restful, or spiritually healthy until we set our hearts on becoming holy.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí la lección debe hablar con franqueza, pues nos hemos acomodado. Como cristianos, con demasiada frecuencia hemos hecho las paces con "bastante bueno" en vez de la santidad. Todos podemos citar: "Por cuanto todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios" (Romanos 3:23) — pero ese versículo describe la necesidad del perdido, y no debemos convertirlo en excusa para que el creyente se acomode en el pecado. Esperamos que el mundo transija; el cristiano no tiene por qué. Nunca seremos felices, reposados, ni espiritualmente sanos hasta que pongamos el corazón en llegar a ser santos.

blocks.en: How Christ Deals with Sin: Penalty, Power, Presence
blocks.es_reference: Cómo Trata Cristo el Pecado: Pena, Poder, Presencia

blocks.en: But someone says honestly, "I believe Jesus forgives my sin; my trouble is that I sin again, and I feel such tendencies to evil within me." Here is a truth that answers that despair. The Lord Jesus came to take away sin in three ways: He came to remove the penalty of sin, the power of sin, and, at last, the presence of sin. These three line up exactly with the three tenses of salvation we have already seen. The penalty of sin was removed when we first believed — this is justification, "I have been saved." The power of sin is being broken day by day as we grow — this is sanctification, "I am being saved." And the presence of sin will be removed entirely when Christ appears — this is glorification, "I will be saved." So the believer who groans over indwelling sin has not been abandoned: forgiveness for the past is his already, power for the future is being supplied now, and full deliverance is certainly coming. Every child of Adam needs two things desperately — forgiveness for the past and power for the future — and in Christ both are given.
blocks.es_reference: Pero alguien dice con sinceridad: "Creo que Jesús perdona mi pecado; mi problema es que vuelvo a pecar, y siento tales tendencias al mal dentro de mí." He aquí una verdad que responde a esa desesperación. El Señor Jesús vino a quitar el pecado de tres maneras: vino a quitar la pena del pecado, el poder del pecado, y, al fin, la presencia del pecado. Estas tres se alinean exactamente con los tres tiempos de la salvación que ya hemos visto. La pena del pecado fue quitada cuando primero creímos — esto es la justificación, "he sido salvo." El poder del pecado se va quebrantando día a día mientras crecemos — esto es la santificación, "estoy siendo salvo." Y la presencia del pecado será quitada por completo cuando Cristo aparezca — esto es la glorificación, "seré salvo." Así que el creyente que gime por el pecado que mora en él no ha sido abandonado: el perdón por el pasado ya es suyo, el poder para el futuro se le suministra ahora, y la plena liberación ciertamente viene. Todo hijo de Adán necesita desesperadamente dos cosas — perdón por el pasado y poder para el futuro — y en Cristo ambas son dadas.

blocks.en: Holiness Needs a New Nature
blocks.es_reference: La Santidad Necesita una Naturaleza Nueva

blocks.en: How then does holiness come? First, it requires a new nature, for our problem runs deeper than behavior.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Cómo viene entonces la santidad? Primero, requiere una naturaleza nueva, pues nuestro problema es más hondo que la conducta.

blocks.en: The cat and the sow. Watch a cat clean itself, washing carefully with tongue and paw — a tidy creature by nature. Now try to teach a sow to do the same. You may scrub it by force, but the moment it is free it hurries back to the mire and is soon as filthy as ever. Why? Cleanliness is contrary to its nature. The only way to get a sow to wash itself is to make it into a cat — change its nature — and then what was impossible becomes easy. So it is with an ungodly man. You may teach him and set him a good example, but he cannot learn the art of holiness, for he has no heart for it. When the Lord makes him a new creature, the new nature pursues what is right as naturally as the old nature wandered after wrong. Only the Holy Spirit can give such a nature.
blocks.es_reference: El gato y la puerca. Observe a un gato limpiarse, lavándose con cuidado con la lengua y la pata — una criatura aseada por naturaleza. Ahora intente enseñar a una puerca a hacer lo mismo. Podrá lavarla por la fuerza, pero en cuanto quede libre corre de vuelta al lodo y pronto está tan sucia como antes. ¿Por qué? La limpieza es contraria a su naturaleza. La única manera de lograr que una puerca se lave es convertirla en gato — cambiar su naturaleza — y entonces lo imposible se vuelve fácil. Así es con el hombre impío. Puede enseñarle y darle buen ejemplo, pero no puede aprender el arte de la santidad, pues no tiene corazón para ello. Cuando el Señor lo hace criatura nueva, la naturaleza nueva persigue lo recto tan naturalmente como la vieja vagaba tras lo malo. Solo el Espíritu Santo puede dar tal naturaleza.

blocks.en: And this new life unfolds as both a crisis and a process. A traveler steps onto a train all at once — that is the crisis, the decisive moment — and then the train carries him nearer and nearer his destination — that is the process. So holiness begins in a moment of new birth and grows over a lifetime of walking with God.
blocks.es_reference: Y esta vida nueva se despliega como crisis y como proceso. Un viajero sube al tren de una vez — esa es la crisis, el momento decisivo — y luego el tren lo lleva cada vez más cerca de su destino — eso es el proceso. Así la santidad comienza en un momento de nuevo nacimiento y crece a lo largo de toda una vida de andar con Dios.

blocks.en: Holiness Needs Desire, Power, and Cleansing
blocks.es_reference: La Santidad Necesita Deseo, Poder y Limpieza

blocks.en: The new nature must be cultivated, and the lesson presses three more needs. First, desire. "Seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness" (Matthew 6:33). It takes time to be holy; no one becomes holy in a hurry, and much of that time must be spent in secret prayer. A seeker once asked an old sage how to find God; the old man held him under the river until he came up gasping, and asked, "While you were under, what did you want most?" "Air!" he cried. "When you want God as much as you wanted air," said the sage, "you will find Him."
blocks.es_reference: La naturaleza nueva debe cultivarse, y la lección insiste en tres necesidades más. Primero, deseo. "Buscad primeramente el reino de Dios y su justicia" (Mateo 6:33). Toma tiempo ser santo; nadie llega a serlo de prisa, y mucho de ese tiempo debe pasarse en oración secreta. Un buscador preguntó una vez a un viejo sabio cómo hallar a Dios; el anciano lo mantuvo bajo el río hasta que salió jadeando, y le preguntó: "Mientras estabas debajo, ¿qué querías más?" "¡Aire!", gritó. "Cuando quieras a Dios tanto como querías el aire," dijo el sabio, "lo hallarás."

blocks.en: Second, power. Why can we not simply fight the devil for a few months and drive him off? Because he is stronger than we are, and will be just as strong at year's end. Trying harder will never break the grip of sin, for our enemy is mightier than our willpower.
blocks.es_reference: Segundo, poder. ¿Por qué no podemos sencillamente pelear contra el diablo unos meses y ahuyentarlo? Porque es más fuerte que nosotros, y lo seguirá siendo al fin del año. Esforzarse más jamás quebrará el dominio del pecado, pues nuestro enemigo es más poderoso que nuestra voluntad.

blocks.en: More machinery than power. A young woman who worked in a great umbrella factory came to her pastor discouraged, fearing she would lose her job. The factory had plenty of orders — but not enough electricity to run all the machines at once, so hers sat idle part of the week. Her trouble, she said, was that the factory had more machinery than power. The early church had little machinery, but it had power. So must we; willpower is not enough, only the power of God.
blocks.es_reference: Más maquinaria que poder. Una joven que trabajaba en una gran fábrica de paraguas vino a su pastor desanimada, temiendo perder su empleo. La fábrica tenía muchos pedidos — pero no suficiente electricidad para mover todas las máquinas a la vez, así que la suya quedaba parada parte de la semana. Su problema, dijo, era que la fábrica tenía más maquinaria que poder. La iglesia primitiva tenía poca maquinaria, pero tenía poder. Así debemos tenerlo nosotros; la fuerza de voluntad no basta, solo el poder de Dios.

blocks.en: Third, cleansing. A minister having a tooth filled complained of the pain as the dentist dug out the decay. "I am going to fill it," the dentist said, "as soon as I get all the impurity out. If I leave any, the filling will not hold, and your peace will soon turn to pain. That is why God insists on a complete cleansing — He is the God of peace, and cannot fully dwell where something will breed discord." And bad habits are best dealt with early, before they grow strong; we say we have habits, but the truth is the habits have us.
blocks.es_reference: Tercero, limpieza. Un ministro a quien le empastaban un diente se quejó del dolor mientras el dentista sacaba la carie. "Voy a empastarlo," dijo el dentista, "en cuanto saque toda la impureza. Si dejo algo, el empaste no se sostendrá, y su paz pronto se volverá dolor. Por eso Dios insiste en una limpieza completa — Él es el Dios de paz, y no puede morar plenamente donde haya algo que engendre discordia." Y los malos hábitos se tratan mejor temprano, antes de que se hagan fuertes; decimos que tenemos hábitos, pero la verdad es que los hábitos nos tienen a nosotros.

blocks.en: Sojourners in Reverent Fear
blocks.es_reference: Peregrinos en Reverente Temor

blocks.en: Peter adds a sober motive for this holy life. "If you call on the Father, who without partiality judges according to each one's work, conduct yourselves throughout the time of your sojourning here in fear" (1 Peter 1:17). The God we call Father is also the Judge who shows no favoritism. So the believer, remembering that he is only a sojourner — a stranger passing through, as we saw in Unit 1 — lives his short stay here in reverent fear, taking God and holiness seriously because he will answer to Him.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro añade un motivo solemne para esta vida santa. "Si invocáis por Padre a aquel que sin acepción de personas juzga según la obra de cada uno, conducíos en temor todo el tiempo de vuestra peregrinación" (1 Pedro 1:17). El Dios a quien llamamos Padre es también el Juez que no hace acepción de personas. Así que el creyente, recordando que es solo un peregrino — un extranjero de paso, como vimos en la Unidad 1 — vive su breve estancia aquí en reverente temor, tomando en serio a Dios y la santidad porque le rendirá cuentas.

blocks.en: Redeemed by the Precious Blood
blocks.es_reference: Redimidos por la Sangre Preciosa

blocks.en: "...you were not redeemed with corruptible things, like silver or gold... but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot." — 1 Peter 1:18-19 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...fuisteis redimidos... no con cosas corruptibles, como oro o plata... sino con la sangre preciosa de Cristo, como de un cordero sin mancha y sin contaminación." — 1 Pedro 1:18-19 (RVG)

blocks.en: And here Peter gives the deepest motive of all for holiness: the price of our rescue. We were not redeemed with corruptible things like silver or gold, nor freed from our empty way of life by any tradition handed down from our fathers, but "with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot." Think of the cost. The Father did not buy us back with the most precious metals of earth, which themselves perish, but with the lifeblood of His spotless Son. This Lamb "was foreordained before the foundation of the world, but was manifest in these last times for you" (1 Peter 1:20) — the plan of redemption is older than creation itself. And through Him we "believe in God, who raised Him from the dead and gave Him glory, so that your faith and hope are in God" (1 Peter 1:21). A people purchased at such a price are not their own; to live carelessly in sin is to despise the blood that bought us.
blocks.es_reference: Y aquí Pedro da el motivo más hondo de todos para la santidad: el precio de nuestro rescate. No fuimos redimidos con cosas corruptibles como oro o plata, ni librados de nuestra vana manera de vivir por tradición alguna heredada de nuestros padres, sino "con la sangre preciosa de Cristo, como de un cordero sin mancha y sin contaminación." Considere el costo. El Padre no nos compró de vuelta con los metales más preciosos de la tierra, que también perecen, sino con la sangre vital de su Hijo sin mancha. Este Cordero "ya estaba destinado desde antes de la fundación del mundo, pero manifestado en los postreros tiempos por amor a vosotros" (1 Pedro 1:20) — el plan de la redención es más antiguo que la creación misma. Y por medio de Él "creéis en Dios, quien le resucitó de los muertos y le ha dado gloria, para que vuestra fe y esperanza sean en Dios" (1 Pedro 1:21). Un pueblo comprado a tal precio no se pertenece a sí mismo; vivir descuidadamente en el pecado es despreciar la sangre que nos compró.

blocks.en: Love from a Pure Heart, Born of the Living Word
blocks.es_reference: Amor de Corazón Puro, Nacidos de la Palabra Viva

blocks.en: Holiness is never merely private; it flowers in love. "Since you have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit in sincere love of the brethren, love one another fervently with a pure heart" (1 Peter 1:22). The same obedience that cleanses the soul knits believers together, and Peter commands a love that is both pure and fervent. Then he reminds them where their new life came from: they have been "born again, not of corruptible seed but incorruptible, through the word of God which lives and abides forever" (1 Peter 1:23). The seed that produced the new birth was the living word. And that word will outlast everything: "All flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of the grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls away, but the word of the LORD endures forever" (1 Peter 1:24-25, quoting Isaiah 40). The world that persecutes the scattered church is itself fading grass; the word that saved them, and the God who spoke it, will stand forever.
blocks.es_reference: La santidad nunca es meramente privada; florece en amor. "Habiendo purificado vuestras almas en la obediencia a la verdad, mediante el Espíritu, para el amor fraternal no fingido, amaos unos a otros entrañablemente, de corazón puro" (1 Pedro 1:22). La misma obediencia que limpia el alma une a los creyentes, y Pedro manda un amor que es a la vez puro y ferviente. Luego les recuerda de dónde vino su vida nueva: han sido "renacidos, no de simiente corruptible, sino de incorruptible, por la palabra de Dios que vive y permanece para siempre" (1 Pedro 1:23). La simiente que produjo el nuevo nacimiento fue la palabra viva. Y esa palabra sobrevivirá a todo: "Toda carne es como hierba, y toda la gloria del hombre como la flor de la hierba. La hierba se seca, y la flor se cae; mas la palabra del Señor permanece para siempre" (1 Pedro 1:24-25, citando Isaías 40). El mundo que persigue a la iglesia esparcida es él mismo hierba que se marchita; la palabra que los salvó, y el Dios que la habló, permanecerá para siempre.

blocks.en: "...having been born again... through the word of God which lives and abides forever." — 1 Peter 1:23 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...renacidos... por la palabra de Dios que vive y permanece para siempre." — 1 Pedro 1:23 (RVG)

sa.prompt: Explain the call to holiness in verses 14-16 and the lesson's warning against spiritual mediocrity.
sa.model: Peter commands the believers, as obedient children, not to be conformed to the former lusts they followed in their ignorance, but to be holy in all their conduct, because it is written, Be holy, for I am holy. The standard is the very character of God: holiness means being set apart and clean, like our Father. The lesson presses this against a comfortable church, warning that we too often settle for pretty good, a spiritual mediocrity, instead of true holiness. We can all quote that all have sinned and fall short, but that verse describes the lost man's need and must never become an excuse for the believer to stay in sin. We expect the world to compromise; the Christian does not have to, and will never be restful or healthy until he sets his heart on becoming holy and refuses to be poured back into the old mold of the flesh.

sa.prompt: Explain the lesson's teaching that Christ takes away sin in three ways — penalty, power, and presence — and how this answers the discouraged believer.
sa.model: The lesson teaches that Christ came to take away sin in three ways: He removes its penalty, its power, and at last its presence. These line up with the three tenses of salvation. The penalty of sin was removed when we first believed, which is justification, I have been saved. The power of sin is being broken day by day as we grow, which is sanctification, I am being saved. And the presence of sin will be removed entirely when Christ appears, which is glorification, I will be saved. This answers the discouraged believer who says, I believe Jesus forgives me, but I sin again and feel evil within. He has not been abandoned: forgiveness for the past is already his, power for the future is being supplied now, and full victory over sin is certainly coming. Every child of Adam needs forgiveness for the past and power for the future, and in Christ both are given.

sa.prompt: Using the cat-and-sow illustration, explain why holiness requires a new nature and is the work of the Spirit.
sa.model: A cat by nature keeps itself clean, washing carefully, but a sow cannot be taught to do the same. You may wash it by force, yet the moment it is free it runs back to the mire, because cleanliness is contrary to its nature. The only way to get a sow to wash itself is to change it into a cat, that is, to change its nature. So it is with an ungodly man. You may instruct him and set him a good example, but he cannot learn the art of holiness, for he has no heart for it; his nature leads him the other way. Only when the Lord makes him a new creature, by the work of the Holy Spirit, does the new nature pursue what is right as naturally as the old wandered after wrong. This is why holiness requires a new nature and cannot be produced by mere effort or instruction; it is the gift of the Spirit, and apart from Him no transformation is possible.

sa.prompt: Describe what the lesson says holiness 'needs' — including desire, power, and cleansing — and the illustrations used.
sa.model: The lesson says holiness needs several things. First it needs desire: we must seek first the kingdom of God, and take time to be holy in secret prayer; as the sage taught the young man held under the river, we will find God when we want Him as much as we wanted air. Second it needs power, for we cannot out-fight the devil, who is stronger than we are and will be just as strong at year's end; trying harder cannot break the grip of sin. The umbrella factory had plenty of machinery but too little electricity, so its machines sat idle; the early church had little machinery but much power, and so must we, for willpower alone is not enough. Third it needs cleansing: like the dentist who must remove all the decay before filling the tooth, God insists on a complete cleansing, and bad habits must be dealt with early, before the habits come to have us.

sa.prompt: Explain verse 13 — preparing the mind and setting hope on grace — and how it connects to the living hope of the previous passage.
sa.model: Verse 13 opens with therefore, linking it to the living hope, inheritance, and salvation just described. Because of that hope, Peter says to gird up the loins of the mind, which in his day meant tucking up a long robe so as not to trip; so we are to pull in loose, lazy thinking and prepare the mind for action. We are to be sober, clear-headed and not intoxicated by the world. And we are to rest our hope fully on the grace that will be brought to us when Jesus Christ is revealed, fixing it not on the comforts of this life but on what is coming. The connection is that the living hope born in us at the new birth is not meant to leave us passive; it is meant to shape how we think and live right now, steadying the mind and anchoring our expectation in the grace yet to come.

sa.prompt: Explain verse 17 — living as sojourners in reverent fear before the impartial Father.
sa.model: Peter says that if we call on the Father, who without partiality judges according to each one's work, we should conduct ourselves throughout the time of our sojourning here in fear. The God we call Father is at the same time the Judge who shows no favoritism and weighs every life honestly. This gives the believer a sober motive for holiness. Remembering that he is only a sojourner, a stranger passing through this world as we saw in the first unit, he lives his short stay here in reverent fear. This is not the cringing terror of a slave but the serious, worshipful awe of a child who takes God seriously, knowing he will give an account. So the exile identity and the call to holiness meet here: because we are strangers who answer to an impartial Father, we walk carefully and reverently while we pass through.

sa.prompt: Explain the redemption described in verses 18-19 — what believers were NOT redeemed with, and what they WERE.
sa.model: Peter gives the deepest motive for holiness by reminding believers of the price of their rescue. They were not redeemed with corruptible things like silver or gold, nor freed from their empty way of life by any tradition handed down from their fathers. Instead they were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. The contrast is striking: the Father did not buy them back even with the most precious metals of earth, which themselves perish, but with the very lifeblood of His spotless Son. This Lamb was foreordained before the foundation of the world and manifested in these last times for them, so the plan of redemption is older than creation. A people purchased at such a cost are not their own, and to live carelessly in sin is to despise the blood that bought them. The price of redemption is therefore a powerful call to a holy life.

sa.prompt: According to verses 20-21, what does Peter say about Christ being foreordained, and where the believer's faith and hope rest?
sa.model: Peter says that Christ, the spotless Lamb, was foreordained before the foundation of the world but was manifested in these last times for the sake of the believers. This means the plan of redemption was settled in the mind of God before creation itself; the cross was no afterthought but the eternal purpose of God, now revealed in history. Then Peter shows where the believer's confidence rests: through Christ they believe in God, who raised Him from the dead and gave Him glory, so that their faith and hope are in God. Their trust is not anchored in themselves or their circumstances but in the God who proved His power and approval by raising Jesus and glorifying Him. Because God raised the Redeemer and crowned Him with glory, the believer's faith and hope stand on the surest possible ground, the living God Himself.

sa.prompt: Explain verses 22-25 — purified souls and fervent love, born of the incorruptible, enduring word of God.
sa.model: Holiness is never merely private; it flowers in love. Having purified their souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit, the believers are commanded to love one another fervently from a pure heart. The same obedience that cleanses the soul knits believers together, and the love Peter calls for is both pure and earnest. He then reminds them where their new life came from: they were born again, not of corruptible seed but incorruptible, through the word of God which lives and abides forever. The living word was the seed that produced the new birth. And that word will outlast everything else, for all flesh is as grass and the glory of man as the flower that withers and falls, but the word of the Lord endures forever. The world that persecutes the scattered church is itself fading grass, while the word that saved them, and the God who spoke it, will stand forever; so they can love boldly and live securely.

sa.prompt: Summarize the central message of Unit 3 (1 Peter 1:13-25).
sa.model: Unit 3 calls the believer from hope to holiness. Because of the living hope, we gird up our minds and rest our hope fully on the grace coming at Christ's revelation, and then we are to be holy as He who called us is holy, refusing the spiritual mediocrity of settling for pretty good. Christ deals with sin completely, removing its penalty, its power, and at last its presence, so the struggling believer has both forgiveness for the past and power for the future. True holiness requires a new nature given by the Spirit, along with desire, power, and a complete cleansing. We live as sojourners in reverent fear, remembering that we were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, the spotless Lamb foreordained before the world. And purified by the truth, we love one another from a pure heart, born again through the living, enduring word of God that outlasts all fading flesh.
